Media theorist Douglas Rushkoff wrote about being invited to lecture for ultra-wealthy men who wanted survival advice for the apocalypse they fear is coming. On Danny Jones's podcast, he expands the episode's premise: elites planning a secret breakaway civilization, and his own invitation to help design it.

Rushkoff describes the questions the rich asked him, about bunkers, loyalty, and control after a collapse, and why the experience changed his view of technology's owners. His account is a memoir of one famous assignment, retold in many places, rather than proof of a single secret program. Jones draws out the wider story of prepping billionaires. Listeners get a rare report from inside the room where the future is being privately hedged against the rest of us.
podcast-joerogan-ZklRSn92ek4:
Biologist Rupert Sheldrake joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 550 to present his theory of morphic resonance. Sheldrake claims that nature learns by habit, that each species shares a memory held outside the brain. His TED talk on science's dogmas was famously pulled, which only grew his fame.

He lays out the evidence he trusts, from animals learning faster worldwide to the sense of being stared at. Rogan asks how the idea could be tested fairly. The episode gives a courteous, full hearing to one of science's most persistent rebels, a man whose name alone starts arguments in faculty rooms.
podcast-dannyjones-jkoDh5htPk4:
Sean Dustin, a recovering crystal meth addict, bares his story to Danny Jones in this episode. Dustin is billed as a real-life Jesse Pinkman, the Breaking Bad character whose life meth destroyed. His account runs from the lab's shadow to rock bottom, then slowly up.

Dustin describes cooking, using, and the crimes and losses that came with addiction. He tells how he finally got clean and what the road back cost him. Jones asks the questions families of addicts most want answered. Recovering and warned listeners get an honest tale from inside the meth world.
podcast-tuckercarlson-7xdsXfxShK4:
Investor Peter Schiff tells Tucker Carlson when he first bought gold. He used bar mitzvah money as a boy of thirteen. That was during the great gold run of the 1970s.

Schiff recalls selling near the top in 1980 by luck. Gold had risen from thirty-five dollars to eight hundred fifty. The title claims gold now beats the S and P index. Schiff argues insiders work to keep savers from noticing. The talk is a gold advocate's full case, told through his own long history with the metal. His faith in gold has never wavered since.
